opus-5.5.text:
I think what's compelling is that it's one of the few times you get to shape a culture from scratch. In academia, or even in a big lab, you inherit a lot: the incentives, the way people talk to each other, what counts as success. When you start something new, every early hire basically writes a piece of that culture.

For me the most exciting part is finding people who are genuinely curious and a bit stubborn in the right way. Research, especially the kind of fundamental work I care about, like visual representation learning and world models, doesn't move forward because someone follows a recipe. It moves forward because someone looks at a result everyone else accepts and says, "Hmm, I don't actually believe that." You want a team full of people like that, but who can also argue openly without it becoming personal.

There's also a sense of shared ownership that's hard to replicate elsewhere. In a small team, everyone can see how their work connects to the mission. There's no layer of abstraction between what you do on Tuesday and whether the whole thing succeeds. That's scary, but it's also really energizing.

And honestly, I've learned that the team *is* the strategy in many ways. Ideas in AI are surprisingly cheap now. Papers come out every day. What's rare is a group of people who trust each other enough to take big bets, fail quickly, and keep going. If you get that right, the specific direction can evolve, and you'll still be okay. If you get it wrong, even a great idea won't save you.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the appeal of building a small team where everyone connects their work to the mission and shares ownership of the outcome.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what's compelling is that you get to choose the people. In academia, you build a lab, but it's shaped a lot by who applies, by funding cycles, by the structure of a PhD program. When you start a company, you're sitting down and asking a much more deliberate question: what are the few things that actually need to be true for this to work, and who are the people I would trust with those things?

For me the thing I keep coming back to is taste. In research, taste is what tells you which problem to work on before the evidence is in. You can't really teach it from a paper. And the best collaborators I've had, going back to my time at FAIR, were people whose judgment I trusted even when they disagreed with me, maybe especially when they disagreed with me. So when I think about a founding team, I'm not really looking for people who can execute what I already believe. I'm looking for a small group where every person has a strong, somewhat different view, and the arguments make the work better.

The other thing that's compelling is the honesty of it. A startup forces you to confront whether the ideas you've been chasing in papers actually matter to anyone outside the community. That's uncomfortable, but it's clarifying. You need people who can live in that discomfort, who are curious enough to keep pushing on the science and grounded enough to care whether something ships.

And honestly, I just like the feeling of a small team at the beginning, before there's a lot of process. Everyone knows everything. Decisions take a conversation instead of a meeting. You see very quickly how good you actually are. That intensity is hard to find anywhere else, and it's a big part of why people do it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes choosing trusted collaborators with different perspectives and caring about whether the work ships, but does not identify bringing people together around a shared mission as a distinctive appeal.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that you’re not just building a product—you’re building a group of people who can figure things out together. At the beginning, there’s so much uncertainty. You don’t necessarily know which ideas will work, so the people you bring in really shape what the company can become.

For me, that’s exciting: finding people who are curious, who have strong opinions but are willing to change their minds, and who bring something that I don’t have. And then creating an environment where they can challenge each other and do work they’re proud of. The team itself becomes a source of new ideas, beyond what any one person could have imagined.

r001.rationale: The response describes the appeal of people figuring things out together and shaping the company, but it does not identify a shared mission as what brings them together.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that you’re not just bringing together people who are individually strong. You’re creating an environment where they can do something together that none of them could do alone. Especially early on, every person changes the team—what questions you ask, how you make decisions, what you consider good enough.

For me, the exciting part is finding people who share a sense of curiosity and ambition but bring different perspectives. You need enough alignment to move together, and enough trust to disagree honestly. When that works, building the team becomes part of the discovery process. You’re figuring out both what to build and how to work together to make it possible.

r001.rationale: The response describes creating something together and having enough alignment to move together, but does not clearly identify a shared mission as the distinctive appeal.
